analysis.one_liner: Makes the expanded Affordable Care Act premium subsidies permanent, so more people qualify and pay less.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 9, 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill has seen no action there while the enhanced premium subsidies it would make permanent expired at the end of 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, people who buy their own health insurance through the ACA marketplaces can claim a federal tax credit that pays most of the premium, but the enhanced version of that credit — larger amounts, and no income ceiling — only ran through 2025. This bill would make the enhanced credit permanent: it deletes the cap that cut people off above four times the federal poverty level, and it lowers the share of their income people must pay toward premiums at every income level. The result is cheaper coverage for millions of marketplace customers, including higher-income households who currently get no help.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage through the ACA marketplaces rather than getting it from an employer or a government program. The bill removes the income ceiling, so households above four times the federal poverty level — currently ineligible for any credit — would qualify again, and at every income level the sliding scale requires people to put a smaller share of their income toward premiums. People just above the old cutoff would see the biggest change, since they currently face full unsubsidized premiums.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on premium tax credit eligibility, which under current law cuts off all help for households above four times the federal poverty level after 2025.
Lowers the applicable percentages — the share of income a household must pay toward a benchmark plan — at every income tier, and ends the scheduled inflation increases to those percentages.
Makes all of these changes permanent; under current law the enhanced credits apply only for 2021 through 2025 and lapse afterward.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a permanent, open-ended increase in the cost of the premium tax credit. Unlike the original temporary enhancements, this version has no expiration date, so the cost continues as long as premiums do. The subsidy money itself is paid to private health insurers as premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the income cap entirely, so higher-income households — some well into six figures — would become newly eligible for federal subsidies, a cost an honest supporter has to defend.

It makes the expanded credit permanent and open-ended, with no expiration or review, rather than the temporary version Congress originally enacted; the Treasury cost grows automatically with premiums.

The bill changes only the size of the tax credit, not the prices insurers charge; the credit is paid toward private plans sold on the exchanges, so it does nothing itself to lower underlying medical costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the help is real and immediate: marketplace premiums went up sharply when the enhanced credits lapsed, and this bill would bring them back down, including for families just above the old income cutoff. The honest cost is fiscal and structural — a permanent open-ended subsidy, newly available to high earners, that pays private insurers and does nothing by itself to slow underlying medical prices. A designed-to-last version might phase the income cap back in or pair the extension with cost controls; this one simply makes the temporary enhancement permanent.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there ever since — no committee vote, no floor action — while the enhanced subsidies it would extend ran out at the end of 2025.

narrative.text: The enhanced premium tax credits created by the American Rescue Plan and Inflation Reduction Act applied only for 2021 through 2025 and lapse after that under current law.
The bill would make those enhancements permanent: no income cap at 400% of poverty, lower required premium contributions at every tier, and no inflation increases to those tiers.
It was introduced January 9, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
Forty-four senators cosponsored the bill — 43 of the 45 Senate Democrats and one of the two Independents; no Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Short term, the federal Treasury avoids the cost of a permanent extension. The people losing out are marketplace customers, who have been paying the full, higher premiums since the enhanced credits lapsed at the end of 2025 with no vote ever held on restoring them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury short-term; marketplace customers pay more

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 9, 2025 to make the enhanced premium tax credits permanent.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 9, 2025 and has not scheduled a markup or any committee action on the bill.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and no Republican has moved it toward a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents and none are Republicans; the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican in a 55–45 Republican Senate.

industries.note: The premium tax credit is paid to private insurers selling plans on the ACA exchanges, so making the enhanced credit permanent locks insurers in as the channel for federal help with premiums and guarantees them a subsidized customer base. Federal rules cap how much of each premium insurers can keep as profit, so their gain rides alongside the gain for the people they cover.
The bill restores subsidy eligibility above 400% of the poverty line, a group currently excluded. Their gain comes at federal cost, which is the bill's main fiscal criticism.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance as introduced. Republicans control the Senate 55–45, no Republican has cosponsored, and the enhanced credits the bill would make permanent have already expired, so the practical question now is whether Congress reinstates them retroactively in a future bipartisan deal rather than passing this bill as written.
